Excerpts are under 15 words and come from a summarizing fetch, so the reviewer re-reads the section named.

sentences.text: Philosophy of history distinguishes speculative questions about the direction or meaning of historical change from critical questions about historical evidence, explanation, narrative, and interpretation.

claims.excerpt: Speculative philosophy of history asks about the meaning and purpose of the historical process.

sentences.text: These inquiries overlap but need not yield a single theory of history.
Giambattista Vico, Johann Gottfried Herder, G. W. F. Hegel, and Karl Marx developed contrasting accounts of historical development.
Hegel associated world history with developing consciousness of freedom; Marx emphasized material production and class struggle.
Critics challenge teleological assumptions and the exclusion of histories that do not fit a single sequence.
Wilhelm Dilthey and R. G. Collingwood examined how historians understand meaningful human actions.
Carl Hempel proposed explanations using general laws, while critics argued that historical accounts often require interpretation of particular intentions, institutions, and contexts.
The debate concerns the relation between causes, reasons, and historical understanding.
Historical narratives select beginnings, endings, agents, and scales.
Hayden White examined narrative forms, while Paul Ricoeur connected narrative with temporality and memory.
Recognition that accounts are constructed does not entail that all accounts are equally well supported: archives, testimony, material traces, and criticism constrain historical claims.
Friedrich Nietzsche and Michel Foucault used genealogy to investigate the contingent formation of values, practices, and institutions.

claims.note: Little names Nietzsche and Foucault in other roles; genealogy is not discussed.

sentences.text: Walter Benjamin questioned triumphalist accounts of progress and emphasized histories of suffering.
Debates about testimony, public memory, and responsibility ask how the past should be represented and acknowledged.
Postcolonial and decolonial historians and philosophers challenge the presentation of European modernity as the universal timeline of human development.
African, Indian, Chinese, and Indigenous historical traditions have developed distinctive approaches to chronology, collective memory, political legitimacy, and transmission.
Comparative work must avoid treating any one as internally uniform.
Contemporary philosophy of history considers global connections, environmental change, historical injustice, and the politics of archives.
Can multiple narratives of the same events be true?
What counts as progress, and for whom?
How do present concerns shape historical inquiry without making it arbitrary?
Philosophy of history asks what history consists of, whether it has a meaning or direction, how historians know and explain the past, and what moral responsibilities the past creates.
Its speculative strand looked for large patterns.

Vico held that a universal human nature shapes the course of nations, Herder that human nature is itself formed by history, Hegel that history is the unfolding of freedom, and Marx that it is driven by developments in production and class conflict.

claims.excerpt: human nature is itself a historical product
claims.fix: reword: Vico's constant human nature and stages; Marx through modes of production

sentences.text: Critics object to the single causes these accounts propose and to finding purpose where no agent directs events.

claims.excerpt: there is no super-agent lying behind historical events

sentences.text: The hermeneutic tradition separated the human sciences from the natural sciences.

Dilthey held that the former rest on understanding meaningful action, the latter on causal explanation, and Collingwood proposed that historians know the past by re-enacting the thought of historical agents.

claims.excerpt: the human sciences were inherently distinct from the natural sciences

sentences.text: Analytic philosophers debated Hempel's covering-law model of 1942, on which historical explanation derives events from general laws; Dray and others argued that history rarely works this way.

claims.excerpt: there are virtually no good examples of universal laws in history
claims.fix: reword to the critics' argument as Little gives it; Dray not named there

sentences.text: From the 1970s Hayden White and Louis Mink turned attention to narrative and to the rhetorical form of historical writing, and Ricoeur linked memory, narrative, identity and history.

claims.excerpt: beginning with the publication of Hayden White's Metahistory (1973)

sentences.text: Reinhart Koselleck's conceptual history studies how the concepts historians use change over time.

claims.excerpt: Koselleck

new_text.section: Speculative and critical philosophy of history
new_text.text: Following W. H. Walsh, philosophers distinguish a speculative philosophy of history, which asks about the meaning and purpose of the historical process, from a critical philosophy of history, which studies historical knowledge, evidence and explanation.

claims.by: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Philosophy of History” (Little, 2025 version, archived) §3
claims.excerpt: Speculative philosophy of history asks about the meaning and purpose of the historical process.

new_text.section: Patterns in history
new_text.text: Vico held that civilizations pass through the same stages because human nature is constant, Herder that human nature is itself a historical product, and Hegel that history is the unfolding of freedom, while Marx traced history through the development of economic modes of production.

claims.by: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Philosophy of History” (Little, 2025 version, archived) §§2.1–2.3
claims.excerpt: human nature is itself a historical product

new_text.section: Patterns in history
new_text.text: Critics find mono-causal interpretations of history vulnerable, and some deny that any super-agent lies behind historical events.

claims.by: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Philosophy of History” (Little, 2025 version, archived) §2.2
claims.excerpt: there is no super-agent lying behind historical events

new_text.section: Kant and Hegel: a plan in history
new_text.text: Kant's essay “Idea for a Universal History with a Cosmopolitan Aim” (1784) begins from the claim that human actions, as appearances, are determined by natural laws, and hopes that history, viewing the play of human freedom as a whole, can find a regular course in it (AA 8:17).

claims.by: Kant, Akademie-Ausgabe vol. 8 (GitHub spookyuser/kant-akademieausgabe-corpus, aa08.txt) p. 17
claims.excerpt: einen regelmäßigen Gang derselben entdecken könne
claims.note: English title as in the Louden and Zöller translation listed in Rauscher's primary sources; date 1784 from the essay's first publication (Berlinische Monatsschrift; Rauscher cites it at AA 8:15–31). AA page read from the Akademie text, not estimated.

new_text.section: Kant and Hegel: a plan in history
new_text.text: In W. Hastie's translation of 1891, the hope is that “a regular march will be discovered” in the movements of human freedom “on the great scale of universal history”.

claims.by: Hastie (1891), OLL text (read through the UMB course mirror of the OLL edition)
claims.excerpt: a regular march will be discovered in its movements

new_text.section: Kant and Hegel: a plan in history
new_text.text: Since individuals and peoples follow no shared plan of their own, Kant proposes to look for a plan of nature in history, “a clue to such a History”, as nature once produced a Kepler and a Newton to find the laws of the planets (AA 8:17–18).

claims.by: Kant, Akademie-Ausgabe vol. 8 (GitHub spookyuser/kant-akademieausgabe-corpus, aa08.txt) pp. 17–18; Hastie (1891), OLL text (read through the UMB course mirror of the OLL edition)
claims.excerpt: a clue to such a History

new_text.section: Kant and Hegel: a plan in history
new_text.text: Nature's means, the Fourth Proposition says, is human antagonism, “the unsocial sociability of men” (AA 8:20); its hardest problem, a perfectly just civil constitution, can only be approached, since “out of such crooked material as man is made of nothing can be hammered quite straight” (AA 8:23).

claims.by: Kant, Akademie-Ausgabe vol. 8 (GitHub spookyuser/kant-akademieausgabe-corpus, aa08.txt) pp. 20, 23 (Vierter, Fünfter, Sechster Satz); Hastie (1891), OLL text (read through the UMB course mirror of the OLL edition)
claims.excerpt: Out of such crooked material as man is made of nothing can be hammered quite straight.
claims.note: Hastie is public domain (1891). German: 'ungesellige Geselligkeit' (8:20); 'aus so krummem Holze ... kann nichts ganz Gerades gezimmert werden' and 'Nur die Annäherung zu dieser Idee ist uns von der Natur auferlegt' (8:23). The just constitution is the Fifth Proposition's problem (8:22), called hardest in the Sixth (8:23).

new_text.section: Kant and Hegel: a plan in history
new_text.text: The Eighth Proposition reads the history of the species as the realisation of “a hidden plan of Nature” (AA 8:27), and the Ninth holds that a philosophical history written by that plan “must be regarded as possible”, while Kant disclaims any wish “to supplant the empirical cultivation of History” (AA 8:29–30).

claims.by: Kant, Akademie-Ausgabe vol. 8 (GitHub spookyuser/kant-akademieausgabe-corpus, aa08.txt) pp. 27, 29–30; Hastie (1891), OLL text (read through the UMB course mirror of the OLL edition)
claims.excerpt: must be regarded as possible, and as even capable of helping forward the purpose of Nature
claims.note: German: 'verborgenen Plans der Natur' (8:27); 'muß als möglich ... angesehen werden' (8:29); 'die Bearbeitung der eigentlichen bloß empirisch abgefaßten Historie verdrängen wollte: wäre Mißdeutung meiner Absicht' (8:30).

new_text.text: Frederick Rauscher, in the Stanford Encyclopedia, ties Kant's view of historical progress to his view of international relations: in this essay incessant wars eventually lead rulers to recognize the benefits of peaceful negotiation, and the argument relies on the self-interest of presumably unelected rulers.

new_text.section: History in the classics on the shelf
new_text.text: Nietzsche's Genealogy offers a principle “for any kind of history” (GM II §12): a thing's origin and its later utility are wholly different matters, since whatever exists is repeatedly “put to new purposes by a force superior to itself”, so that understanding a custom's present use, punishment's for example, gives no understanding of its origin.

new_text.section: History in the classics on the shelf

new_text.section: History in the classics on the shelf

new_text.section: Understanding and explanation
new_text.text: Dilthey held the human sciences to be inherently distinct from the natural sciences, with the understanding of meaning as their method, and Collingwood presented re-enacting the thought of historical agents as the way historians know the past.

new_text.section: Understanding and explanation
new_text.text: In The Idea of History, published after his death in 1946, Collingwood separates the outside of an event from its inside, “that in it which can only be described in terms of thought”, and treats an action as the unity of the two.

new_text.section: Understanding and explanation
new_text.text: James Connelly, in the Stanford Encyclopedia, explains that the historian re-enacts “the very same thought as the agent”, a thought identified by its content.

claims.excerpt: they do not re-enact a thought of a similar kind but the very same thought as the agent

new_text.section: Understanding and explanation
new_text.text: Kuukkanen quotes Collingwood's dictum that “all history is the history of thought” and gives the example of Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon, which a description of bodily movements leaves unexplained.

claims.excerpt: Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon can be described as a set of bodily movements

new_text.section: Understanding and explanation
new_text.text: Critics associated re-enactment with Dilthey's empathy and charged it with crediting historians with telepathic access to other minds (Connelly cites Patrick Gardiner, 1952); Connelly replies that the doctrine makes a conceptual point about what historians re-enact and prescribes no empathetic method, and he takes up the objection that it over-rationalizes the subject matter of history.

claims.excerpt: It is not meant to prescribe to historians an empathetic method

new_text.section: Understanding and explanation
new_text.text: Carl Hempel's 1942 essay modelled historical explanation on covering laws; critics replied that historical explanations resemble explanations of individual behaviour, and that history offers virtually no good examples of universal laws.

claims.by: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Philosophy of History” (Little, 2025 version, archived) §3.1
claims.excerpt: there are virtually no good examples of universal laws in history

new_text.section: Understanding and explanation
new_text.text: In that essay Hempel held that “general laws have quite analogous functions in history and in the natural sciences”, so that explaining a historical event means subsuming it under laws.

claims.excerpt: The pivotal feature of Hempel's model is thus its appeal to general laws.

new_text.section: Understanding and explanation
new_text.text: W. H. Dray answered with a rational-action model of explanation (1957), on which historians explain an action through the agent's reasons, and, Connelly reports, argued that Hempel failed to see what distinguishes explaining actions from explaining events.

claims.excerpt: Dray argued that Hempel failed to see that what distinguishes action from event explanations
claims.note: Kuukkanen dates Dray's rational-action theory 1957 in §3.1.1 (cited) and 1963 in §2.2; 1957 is Laws and Explanation in History.

new_text.section: Understanding and explanation
new_text.text: Hempel (1974) maintained that even explanations of particular actions presuppose law-like generalizations; later critics, Kuukkanen reports, held that the debate concerned forms of explanation irrelevant to practising historians.

claims.excerpt: often focused on forms of explanation irrelevant to the concerns of practicing historians

claims.by: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Philosophy of History” (Little, 2025 version, archived) §§1.3, 3.4
claims.excerpt: beginning with the publication of Hayden White's Metahistory (1973)

new_text.section: Narrative and concepts
new_text.text: Reinhart Koselleck asked philosophers of history to identify the concepts needed to characterize history, such as the space of experience and the horizon of expectation, to place them in their political and social discourses, and to assess how useful they are.

claims.by: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Philosophy of History” (Little, 2025 version, archived) §2.5

new_text.section: Recent directions

claims.by: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Philosophy of History” (Little, 2025 version, archived) §§1.2–1.3, 4
